quote: In the eighth place locusts are mentioned. Some interpreters think that this sort of plague confutes the inconstancy of the human race, filled with dissent and discord. In another sense, the locusts can be interpreted as representing flittering mobility, like the pleasures of this world in a restless and skittish soul.
source_title: QUESTIONS ON THE OLD TESTAMENT, EX 14:14

quote: And the briefly recorded fact that the heart of Pharaoh experienced a kind of softening when he said, "But you shall not proceed far; you shall go a three days' journey and leave your wives behind," and whatever else he spoke when yielding before the marvelous works makes it clear that these signs had some effect even on him, though they did not entirely accomplish their object. Yet not even this would have happened if the idea held by most people about the words, "I will harden Pharaoh's heart," rightly represented what was wrought by him, that is, by God.

Even the locust, by divine grace, penetrates everywhere, and when it has filled the width of each region with its dense swarm, it first strikes without harm, and feeds on the barren land only after receiving the divine signal of permission. Indeed, just as we read in Exodus, it also acts as the celestial executor of righteous vengeance.

But that mention is made of locusts in the eighth place, I think that through this kind of plague the inconstancy of the human race, ever at variance with itself and discordant, is confuted. For the locust, though it has no king, as Scripture says: "leads forth its army arrayed in one battle-line"; but men, though made rational by God, have been able neither to govern themselves in ordered fashion nor to bear patiently the guidance of God their king.

In the ninth plague, darkness fell. Either it means the blindness of their minds or that they should realize that the workings of the divine economy and of providence are most obscure. For God made darkness his hiding place. But they desired boldly and rashly to investigate it and, drawing one conclusion after another, fell into the dense and palpable darkness of ignorance.
source_title: QUESTIONS ON THE OLD TESTAMENT, EX 14:15

quote:
We say, lest perhaps also the "palpable darkness" in Egypt was made in this manner for "three days", not from an eclipse of the sun, but either because dark clouds ran together into one, or because the air there then became thicker over the Egyptians only — for "to all the sons of Israel", as the scripture testifies, "there was light in all the places in which they were dwelling".

For it is also impossible in an eclipse of the sun, which happens from the coming together of the moon to the sun, for darkness to be made for "three" continuous "days"; and it would be believed that there was some other cause of the darkness in Egypt, if the sun had even been named, or as though darkened at that time. But now the scripture of Exodus says nothing else except that "Moses stretched out his hand to heaven, and there was darkness and gloom and the rest over the whole land of Egypt for three days;…

The ninth plague is darkness, whether so that the blindness of their mind may be convicted, or so that they may understand that the reasons of the divine dispensation and providence are most obscure. For "God has made darkness his hiding-place", which they, desiring boldly and rashly to search out, and asserting one thing from another, have been rolled down into the thick and "palpable darkness" of errors.
